title: Controllers & routing: order, status codes, @Res() and versions
objectives: Predict which handler a request reaches when `:id` is declared before a literal path, and fix it by ordering or with Nest 12's `routeConflictPolicy` / `routeResolutionStrategy`
Predict the default status for a handler (200, or 201 for POST) and change it with `@HttpCode`, `@Header`, `@Redirect` or an exception
Explain what `@Res()` makes your job (sending the response) and what it throws away (interceptor output, serialization), and use `passthrough: true` instead
Version routes with `enableVersioning`, controller and `@Version` metadata, `VERSION_NEUTRAL` and `defaultVersion`, and predict which requests 404

questions.prompt: `UsersController` declares `@Get(":id") findOne()` and, below it, `@Get("me") findMe()`. On the default Express adapter, what does `GET /users/me` run?

options.text: `findOne`, with `id` set to `"me"` — the first registered route whose pattern matches wins
`findMe` — Nest prefers a literal path over a parameter
Nothing: Nest refuses to start because the two routes conflict
Both handlers, in declaration order

questions.explanation: Nest registers routes in declaration order and Express tries them in that order, so the first pattern that matches gets the request — and `:id` matches any one segment, `me` included. Preferring the literal is what Fastify's router does, and what Nest 12's opt-in `routeResolutionStrategy: "specificity"` does on Express. A boot error only happens if you opt in with `routeConflictPolicy: { shadow: "error" }`; by default the app starts silently.

questions.prompt: `@Get(":id") findOne(@Param("id", ParseIntPipe) id: number)` is declared above `@Get("recent") recent()`. `GET /orders/recent` returns 400 "Validation failed (numeric string is expected)". What's the fix?

options.text: Declare `recent` above `:id` (or turn on Nest 12's `routeResolutionStrategy: "specificity"`) — the router chose `findOne` before the pipe ran
`new ParseIntPipe({ optional: true })`, so a non-numeric id falls through to the next route
Register a global `ValidationPipe({ transform: true })` so `"recent"` is coerced first
Catch the 400 in an exception filter and call `recent()` from there

questions.explanation: Routing picks the handler first; pipes run afterwards, on that handler's arguments. A pipe can convert or reject a value, but it can't send the request to a different route — there is no fall-through. The 400 is `ParseIntPipe` correctly rejecting `"recent"` as an id, which makes a routing bug look like a validation bug. Fix the order (literal before parametric), or let Nest 12 order by specificity.

questions.prompt: A `@Post("login")` handler returns a token, and a `@Delete(":id")` handler returns nothing. With no other decorators, what statuses do clients get?

options.text: 201 for the login, and 200 with an empty body for the delete
200 for the login, 204 for the delete
201 for the login, 204 for the delete
200 for both

questions.explanation: Nest's default is 200 for every route except POST, which is 201 — whatever the handler does. It doesn't inspect the body either, so a delete that returns nothing is a 200 with an empty body, not a 204. A login creates no resource, so `@HttpCode(200)` says what you mean there; `@HttpCode(204)` does the same for the delete.

questions.prompt: `PUT /orders/:id` should answer 201 when it created the order and 200 when it replaced one. How?

options.text: Take `@Res({ passthrough: true }) res`, call `res.status(created ? 201 : 200)`, and return the order
Put `@HttpCode(created ? 201 : 200)` on the method
Take `@Res() res`, call `res.status(...)`, and return the order
Throw `new HttpException(order, 201)` when it was created

questions.explanation: Decorators run once at startup, so `@HttpCode()` takes a fixed value — `created` isn't even in scope there. Plain `@Res()` gives you `res.status()` but makes sending your job: returning the order leaves the request hanging. `passthrough: true` gives you the response object for the status *and* lets Nest send your return value through interceptors and serialization. Throwing `new HttpException(order, 201)` does send a 201, but down the error path: interceptors' `map` and `ClassSerializerInterceptor` never see the order, and a catch-all exception filter (error logging, alerting) reports a success as a failure.

questions.prompt: A controller uses `ClassSerializerInterceptor`, and `User.passwordHash` carries `@Exclude()`. One handler is rewritten as `me(@Res() res: Response) { res.json(this.users.current()); }`. What does the client receive?

options.text: The user **with** `passwordHash`: `res.json()` serialized it before any interceptor could, and Nest discards what interceptors produce in this mode
The user without `passwordHash` — controller-level interceptors apply to every handler
Nothing; Nest refuses to boot a controller that mixes `@Res()` and interceptors
The user with `passwordHash`, because interceptors are skipped completely — a timing interceptor on it stops logging too

questions.explanation: With `@Res()` you send the bytes yourself. Nest still runs the interceptor chain — a timing or logging interceptor still fires (checked on Nest 11.2 and 12.1) — but the handler returns `undefined`, the JSON has already gone out, and whatever the interceptor maps is thrown away. So `@Exclude()` never gets a chance. Return the object (or use `passthrough: true`) and the serializer works again.

questions.prompt: The app calls `enableVersioning({ type: VersioningType.URI })`, and `HealthController` has no version, so the load balancer checks `GET /health`. Someone adds `defaultVersion: "1"`. What happens to that check?

options.text: It starts failing with 404: the unversioned controller is now version 1 and lives at `/v1/health`
Nothing — `defaultVersion` only applies to requests that don't name a version
It keeps working; the route now answers at both `/health` and `/v1/health`
Nest refuses to start until every controller declares a version

questions.explanation: `defaultVersion` versions *routes*, not requests: every route without its own version becomes version 1, and under URI versioning that means a `/v1` segment. Paths that must never move — health checks, webhooks, anything a third party calls — get `version: VERSION_NEUTRAL`: under URI versioning it has no version segment, so no `defaultVersion` can move it (and `/v1/health` stays a 404).

questions.prompt: `@Controller({ path: "cats", version: "1" })` contains `@Version("2") @Get(":id") findOne()`. URI versioning is on. Which requests reach `findOne`?

options.text: Only `GET /v2/cats/:id` — a route's version replaces the controller's
`/v1/cats/:id` and `/v2/cats/:id` — the versions add up
Only `/v1/cats/:id` — the controller's version wins
Neither; conflicting versions make the route unreachable

questions.explanation: Route-level version metadata overrides any version that would otherwise apply, the controller's included, so v1 clients now get a 404 for `/v1/cats/:id`. If both should keep it, list both: `@Version(["1", "2"])`.

questions.prompt: `CatsV1Controller` and `CatsV2Controller` both use `path: "cats"`, with `version: "1"` and `version: "2"`. `main.ts` never calls `enableVersioning()`. What does `GET /cats` do?

options.text: The first registered controller answers every request; v2 is unreachable, and nothing warns you
404 — the request names no version
v2 answers, as the latest version
Nest refuses to start: two controllers claim the same path

questions.explanation: Without `enableVersioning()` the version metadata is ignored, so both controllers register plain `GET /cats` and the first one registered gets every request. Nest 12 can catch this at boot with `routeConflictPolicy: { duplicate: "error" }` — it reports two routes with the same method, path, host and version — but only if you turn it on.

prompts.prompt: Declare these so `GET /users/me` reaches `findMe` on the default Express adapter, without any Nest 12 options.
prompts.explanation: Nest registers routes in declaration order and Express takes the first match, so the literal path goes first and the one-segment catch-all `:id` after it. The parameter route would match `me` too, which is exactly why it can't come first.

prompts.prompt: Answer a successful delete with 204, mark a report as never cacheable, and send readers who ask for version 5 to the old docs instead of the decorator's URL.
prompts.explanation: `@HttpCode()` replaces the default status (200, or 201 for POST) and `@Header()` adds a fixed response header; both are read once at startup, so their values can't depend on the request. `@Redirect()` is the exception that takes a runtime override: return `{ url, statusCode }` and it replaces the decorator's arguments, while returning nothing keeps them (the status defaults to 302 when the decorator omits it). For a runtime success status elsewhere, use `@Res({ passthrough: true })`; for an error, throw.

prompts.prompt: Set a session cookie but leave sending to Nest, so interceptors and serialization still apply to the returned user.
code: async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto, @Res({ ___: true }) res: Response) {
res.cookie("session", token, { httpOnly: true, secure: true });
prompts.explanation: Without `passthrough`, injecting `@Res()` makes sending your job and Nest ignores the return value — this handler would hang. With it you get the response object for the cookie, and the returned `user` still goes through interceptors and `ClassSerializerInterceptor`.

prompts.prompt: Put the version in the path, make this controller version 2, and keep the health check out of versioning.
prompts.explanation: URI versioning serves the controller at `/v2/cats` (after any global prefix). Under URI versioning a `VERSION_NEUTRAL` route has no version segment (under header versioning it answers any version or none), so a later `defaultVersion` can't move `/health` under `/v1`.

prompts.prompt: Nest 12: refuse to start when one route shadows another — or, instead, have Nest register literal segments before parametric ones whatever the declaration order.
prompts.explanation: Both options are new in Nest 12 and off by default. `"error"` collects every conflict into one `RouteConflictException` from `app.init()`, so a boot (an e2e run, a deploy) fails loudly; `"warn"` only logs. `"specificity"` reorders registration so `me` beats `:id` (the default is `"declaration"`). On Fastify, whose router already ranks by specificity, `shadow` and `"specificity"` do nothing — only `duplicate` applies there.

code: findOne(@Param("id") id: string) { return { handler: "findOne", id }; }
// Nest 12 on Express, no routing options set. Request: GET /users/profile
snippets.question: What status and body does the client get?
snippets.explanation: Shadowing doesn't stop at a class boundary. `UsersController` comes first in the module's `controllers` array, so its `/users/:id` is registered before `ProfileController`'s `/users/profile`, and Express hands the request to the first match. Swap the array order, move `profile` into the same controller above `:id`, or set Nest 12's `routeResolutionStrategy: "specificity"`. `routeConflictPolicy: { shadow: "warn" }` would have printed this exact pair at boot.

code: return summary;          // used to be res.json(summary)
snippets.question: A refactor changed the last line. What does the client get now?
snippets.answer: No response at all — the request hangs until the client times out
snippets.explanation: Injecting `@Res()` puts the handler in library-specific mode: sending is your job, and Nest ignores the return value — no 200, no error, nothing (checked on Nest 11.2 and 12.1 with Express). Interceptors even run and their output is discarded too. Delete the `@Res()` parameter and return the value, or use `@Res({ passthrough: true })` if you still need the response object.

snippets.question: What status does that request get?
snippets.explanation: `defaultVersion` gives a version to *routes* that don't declare one; it doesn't give one to a *request* that doesn't send the header. A header-less request matches no versioned route, so even the v1 controller doesn't answer (verified on Nest 12.1.3). If "no header means v1" is the contract, implement it with a `VersioningType.CUSTOM` extractor that returns `"1"` when the header is missing.
